utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated. Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, once more, I would like to know whether even today you can follow the proceedings in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please sit down. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsels, Mr. Jose Doria and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Vasvija Vidovic, with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence of Mr. Naser Oric. With us there also are legal assistant, Adisa Mehic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good afternoon to you and your team. Preliminaries, I think I have one matter to raise myself, on behalf of the Bench of course. You have filed, Mr. Wubben, an application -- sorry I call it an application, for the issuance of subpoena ad testificandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into private session on this. All I want to know for the time being, I'm not going to mention any witnesses, et cetera, you know, which witness we are referring to, whether there is -- whether we are to expect a response from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is our position in this case, as in the case so far, when the -- that we will not submit any submissions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Things being like that, then we have already discussed amongst ourselves, and we are in a position to hand down the decision, which will be handed down this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I thank, Your Honours. We're much obliged because we want to proceed on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Wubben, the Trial Chamber is always doing its best to meet its commitments without any undue delay, and this is one further instance. The other thing is this. Much to my surprise, and also in the few minutes we've had to discuss, I can tell you also the surprise of my two colleagues, we have been informed that you have today decided to drop expert witness, Mr. Turle or Colonel Turle. Of course, we cannot interfere with your discretion to do that, neither can the Defence. If you have decided to withdraw this witness, it's your business. But the thing is this: You owe us at least an explanation as to how this is going to affect the schedule, the work schedule, in the near and in the -- in the near and in the distant future, which, in turn, brings me to perhaps the most important part of the matter that I wanted to raise, and that is, we have waited -- we waited the entire -- the whole of last week to have sort of a projection of the rest of the case of the Prosecution, and we agreed, together with -- you were not here last week -- we agreed with Mr. Di Fazio and Madam Sellers, that we will, albeit reluctantly, await until the middle of this week. We are almost there. We will not wait beyond Wednesday, Mr. Wubben. That's tomorrow. So, we will need to know, at the latest tomorrow, what the projection of the rest of the case of the Prosecution is, or looks like. That's number 1. Now, let's go through these two points one by one. You have decided to withdraw this witness, this expert witness. All right. How is it going to affect the rest of the case, or the immediate -- he was supposed to come between the 19th and the 22nd, to be called between the 19th and 22nd of April, of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 18th to 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 18 to 21st anyway. It was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either 18th to 21st or 19th to 22nd. 18th to 21st, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Upon deciding the first, what I did was to inform Defence counsel, then the legal officer. And including that also, to try to find out opportunities to modify, reschedule for the next week. We tried to do so, but as this is a latest development based upon the overall assessment of the developments in the evidence in our case so far, we can only try to do from the -- this afternoon, to do our best in that respect. And we will, of course, update you and the Defence, because for the Defence it will mean that whenever there is a new witness coming in, anticipated in the later stage, then the Defence should have time enough to prepare. These kinds of circumstances I will anticipate and consider as well in order to update you and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's as if we are speaking two different languages, Mr. Wubben. Let me make myself clear. Today, which is the 12th, we are starting with the testimony of Milosava Nikolic. Now, Ms. Richardson, how long do you think you will be examining this witness in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the examination-in-chief, I would hope to end by this session, hopefully, depending on how slowly this witness -- how we proceed. She can't sit for long periods of time, but she has assured me that she will endure at least an hour and a half sitting. So I am hoping that by the end of today's session to complete my examination-in-chief, and of course the Defence will have tomorrow. The following witness is the Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How long is that going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's another crime-based witness and that witness will be taken by Ms. Sellers, and we anticipate that he will be completed by Friday, no later than Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, which brings us to the following week, which is next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would have started with precisely Colonel Turle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm saying, there is less than a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we completely understand what the Bench is trying to convey. What we are in the process of doing at the moment is contacting witnesses that were scheduled to come in later on and to see if one of those witnesses can be -- we can sort of get them here sooner so we can have a witness for the Trial Chamber starting either Tuesday or Wednesday, and that's what we're in the process -- at this time we're doing at the moment, contacting these individuals to see who can come in on such short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that means we are losing another day, Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, what I can also assure the Court is that we have been working vigorously to try and assess how much longer our case will continue, and what we have so far is that, not only have we dropped our expert witness, but there might be one or two other witnesses that we may decide not to call and so we will not lose time. Indeed, we may very well meet the Court's dead line and end our case by the end of May. So the fact that we are not calling this witness and we are losing time, it will not impact on how much longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have made very, very careful calculated assessment of the time and taken into consideration what Your Honour has stated previously, last week, to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I confirm, because that addressed the second issue that you anticipated to trigger, and that will be, indeed, the outcome of an assessment of the scheduling and the witness projected. And, as such, we have new developments and some of the developments might turn out and clarify to us no earlier than Wednesday, but we can, indeed -- and I can confirm what Ms. Richardson stated to the court, I can confirm that these three days will not be anticipated as damaging the schedule. And we are trying to make that huge step, as you requested to the Defence team last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is, it's still -- in my mind, you know, I mean, and I'm speaking out of experience now and out of no other consideration, I can assure you, but today is Tuesday. I am getting the impression that you still haven't got a clear indication as to who could start giving evidence Tuesday, today week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Of course not at this moment; otherwise, I would have informed you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which takes us to Wednesday. That's tomorrow. Which would mean you have to make arrangements to get this person to come over, and that would take us probably Friday, knowing when witnesses come and go, which would mean proofing on Saturday and on Sunday and of course Monday, because already we've had the message sent loud and clear that Monday will be needed by you. And what about the Defence? They are probably not going to know until Wednesday, at least, minimum Wednesday, if not Thursday, which witness they will have next in line. This is what worries me, you know. I mean, we've tried to work with you, treating you with silk gloves all along, all along, both the Prosecution and Defence. But as we approach the deadline that needs to be fixed for a determination of your case, and the commencement of the case of the Defence, if we get to that stage, we can't allow a situation to fluctuate from one day to the other like this, you know. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's very precarious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, we are very much aware of the due process concerns, and what we are doing at this point, as we speak, other members of the team are contacting witnesses who are supposed to follow Colonel Turle, and so the Defence will not be, we're hoping, too inconvenienced by having to be prepared for the next two witnesses who are supposed to come the following weeks. So we're trying to keep within the schedule, Your Honour, and not take it so far out that the process will be impacted upon the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, tomorrow is Wednesday and we will need to hear more from you, Mr. Wubben particularly, as to how you are planning the schedule for the rest of your case. And I know that you will cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I will give you some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not let you not, either. Yes, Mr. Jones, sorry, I did not ask you to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obviously, there is an ongoing process, but I thought to give you our brief reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obviously, in terms of dropping a witness, that in itself doesn't create any grave problem, apart from I personally regret the loss of a great number of hours during this unseasonally fine weather which we have been having in The Hague preparing for a witness that won't come. But that obviously in itself isn't the issue. There are really three concerns. One is whether there's going to be a new military expert that the Prosecution is going to bring forward or whether they're simply not going to call one. That's of concern because, firstly, the case has been presented according to a certain theory. We've reacted to that theory in accordance with what we believe the expert testimony would be. We've instructed our own expert, who has prepared a report, which reacts to the Prosecution's report. So, of course, if there is a new expert, if there are new theories of the case which the Prosecution is presenting, it has implications for how we would have presented our case. It has implications for briefing our expert. Again, whether we'll get funding for that. That's one host issue which I just wish to flag up, lest it be thought that a new expert may simply be substituted without detriment to us. The second issue is, the witness who will come next week, and I think Your Honour has perfectly appreciated the difficulty to us if all of a sudden, particularly an important witness, is going to come forward. But the Prosecution, I understand, also appreciates that we need to know as soon as possible. But the third concern is just this: That the Prosecution has indicated that, despite witnesses being dropped, that the Prosecution case will nonetheless probably be finish on time. But I do feel bound to point out that we've also been notified the Prosecution intends to bring new witnesses. We were notified of four already. And if, at this stage, the Prosecution is having a rethink of its whole case and it's going to drop witnesses and apply to add new ones, it's not necessarily a pure numbers exercise that, Well, you had ten witnesses and here are ten other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it's not a pure numbers exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. All of this remains to be seen, but I just wanted to mention our concerns at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I anticipate, on the basis of what happened in other cases before this Tribunal, when the Prosecution asked for the production of fresh evidence at the late stage in its case and before its conclusion, the conclusion of its case, in many cases it hasn't been easy to decide. So, I'm in no way indicating that it's going to be plain sailing, because the system, how it works here, with the pre-trial brief and the way the parties are expected to administer a case, their respective case, makes it important or imperative on the Trial Chamber to be careful in granting such requests. Also there is -- I'm making myself very clear, because we, of course, don't know what your request as regards fresh evidence is going to be. We still have to see the motion and also see what the grounds for your application will be. But also, you need to keep in mind that if you are going to combine your application with a declaration that you are dropping some witnesses, with the consequence that, therefore, the case will not last longer, if you combine the two together. Please do keep in mind that if ultimately we decide not to grant the motion, we will not allow you then to go back on your declaration of withdrawal of witnesses. So, in other words we are not hiding anything from you. We are dealing with you in the most transparent manner. If you combine the two, you will have to accept the consequences should we decide not to grant the motion. We are not saying of course that we will not grant the motion, especially not knowing what the position taken by the Defence will be, and not knowing what the reasons for your applications will be, and how much this will be in the interest of justice to grant. Obviously, I mean, it's all in a vacuum. But we will see. But I want you to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am aware, and we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. So let's bring in the witness. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to welcome you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before I continue, I want to make sure, first, that you are comfortable in that chair and, secondly, that you are receiving interpretation in your own language. Are you comfortable in that chair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps, usher, if she moves -- if she is moved a little bit further -- or if you move -- I don't know. Anyway, leave it for the time being. Are you receiving interpretation in your own language, of what is being said in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam, if at any time there is a problem with the interpretation, tell us straight away and we will make sure that it is rectified before we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at me, I am the Presiding Judge in this trial, which has been instituted against Naser Oric. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from the island of Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt, from the Kingdom of Denmark, and to my left I have and Judge Albin Eser from Germany.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you are soon going to start giving evidence, and our Rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration, something like an oath, in the sense that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. In order to help you make this declaration, I am going to ask you to remain seated where you are. You don't need to stand up. And I am going to dictate the declaration to you. Each time I dictate a part of it, please repeat it after me. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- when you have concluded, that will be your solemn declaration. I am going to start now. I, Milosava Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please repeat what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milosava Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell the truth about everything I know, as I always have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole truth. Don't add any words. Just repeat my words. The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, nothing but the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. I will explain to you, very briefly, the procedure. You are now going to be asked a few questions by Madam Richardson. You've met Madam Richardson and she is a member on the Prosecution team in this case. When she is finished, you will then be asked some questions by Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel in the Defence of Naser Oric. I want to make sure that during your testimony you are feeling comfortable all the time. So if, at any time, you're not feeling well, or you would like a break, please do not hesitate to tell us straight away and we will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and we will have a break immediately. You've got some water there in case you are thirsty, and Madam Usher will be assisting you during the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. [Trial Chamber confers with legal officer and usher]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me say it and then it can be translated to her. Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, I think you will be sitting more comfortable if you moved back a little bit in your chair, so that you can rest your back, all right? And don't be afraid of those two microphones that you have in front of you, they have harmed nobody as yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I think that the ELMO, Madam Usher, is in the way of Ms. Richardson, so it's in the way, definitely. I think we will need to move it. All right. That's fine. Yes, madam Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Can you state your full name for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Milosava Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Can you please confirm, with a yes the following questions that I am about to ask you. So if you listen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With a yes or no. Were you born on June 27th, 1933?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Yes, I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you are of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you are married to Milorad Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you have three children?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We have three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you live in a hamlet of Popovici?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Which is the village of Opravdici?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The hamlet of Popovici consists of approximately 25 houses; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And my question, with respect to the number of houses, relates to the period of time, 1992 to January of 1993. Were there approximately 25 houses during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time there were exactly 25 houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And there are approximately 100 or so persons living in your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, your husband, Milorad, and yourself, you farmed for a living? And that you --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we still farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also have livestock, including sheep?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to bring your attention to 1992, just before 1993. So what I would like to ask is whether or not you were aware that there was a conflict in Bosnia that began in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew -- I knew that it came.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I would like to ask you about the location of Popovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have maps for everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richardson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the villagers went Zelinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I haven't asked anything yet. I'm handing out maps for the members of the Defence and the judges. So if you will bear with us for a moment so everyone can see where your village and hamlet is located. Now, the village of -- now, your village, your hamlet in fact, Popovici, is located on a hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the closest Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And approximately how far is Glogova from Popovici, by foot?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Maybe an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that the usher put this map on the ELMO. I'm not going to ask the witness to look at it. She can't read and will not be of assistance, but just in case we need to at some point for demonstrative purposes only, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, with respect to Glogova, were you aware that any type of conflict had taken place in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this conflict? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In 1993. This is when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me bring your attention to January of 1993. Do you recall that particular month and year?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I know, I will remember. What I don't know, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, on the 7th of January, 1993, did anything happen in the neighbouring village? Not in your village, but in any of the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Mandici, Mandici and Kravica burned down on the 7th. Mandici and Kravica burned down and all the livestock was driven away from Mandici, in the evening, at 5.00. And they started cursing us and swearing at us, and they told us that they would come back for us on the following day. That was on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How is it that you were able to see -- well, I will rephrase that question. Were you able to see the village of Mandici from your village of Popovici?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course we could see it. It's close. We could see each other. We could call out to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is Mandici also located on a hill?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said the houses -- I will rephrase. What were you able to see from your village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We could see fire. We could see houses ablaze and we could see livestock being driven away, and the villagers of Mandici fled to our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you see who was driving the livestock away?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Troops came by and they set houses on fire and drove away the cattle. I don't know what troops they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity the -- the ethnicity of the troops? Were they Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what their ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is Mandici a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You said the people from Mandici came to your village. Did they say anything to you about what had happened in their village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They came to our village, and they were watching from our village their houses burning and their livestock being driven away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified that something had been said to you about tomorrow. Could you just repeat for the Trial Chamber what it was that you heard said about your village.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was said for our village? As they were driving the cattle away, the cattle from Mandici, when they burned Mandici, then they said, We'll fuck your Serbian mother. We will come back for you tomorrow. And they did. They came back for us on the 8th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before we go to the 8th of January, were you able to see if there were any other villages, other than Mandici, burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see Kravica or other villages on the 7th. I only saw Mandici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said they were taking the cattle away. What direction were these people taking the cattle in?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took the cattle from two households. They took cows, and these people were watching their houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what direction did they take the cattle? What direction did they take? Did they go towards a particular village or a particular area? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They went towards Glogova. They took the road that leads to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did the -- after observing what you saw in Mandici take place, what did -- what did you do and the other villagers from Popovici do?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mandici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What we did? We went to Zelinje. All of us went there. Nobody spent the night there. And then we returned to tend to our livestock. Then they surrounded us. They started shooting at us. They started burning houses. Those who could flee, fled. And I stayed behind. I couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, specifically, I would like to ask you about the 7th. What did you do after you observed the village of Mandici burning? Did you take any action? Did you stay in your village? Or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All the people from Mandici, Popovici and Kravica, we all went to Zelinje. Nobody stayed behind. On the following morning, some of the people returned home to see about their cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you also return?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did, as well as my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many other villagers returned to the village on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The six of us returned. And when they started shooting, these people ran away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, let me ask you: Is the 7th and 8th of January of any significance to someone who is Serb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can put a direct question straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is the 7th of January, 1993 the Serb Orthodox holiday? Christmas, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Christmas. Orthodox Christmas. Our Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, bringing you back to the 8th of January, 1993, when you returned home, could you tell us what time you returned home?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We got there around half past nine, half past nine. We tended to our cattle. And then they started shooting at us. And people started looking for a hiding place. I returned to tend to my sheep. Around 2.00 I got captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me bring you back to the time of the shooting. Do you remember, was that at half past nine, or later?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At half past 10, the first shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you with your husband at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He went to tend to the oxen and I went to tend to the sheep and I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you first heard the shooting, could you tell us, what was the -- did you hear one shot, or more than one?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There was a lot. Not just one shot. There were many, and those who could run away, they did. And those who couldn't, they got killed. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell what -- the direction that the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From everywhere. I can't say that it came from only one direction. There was shooting from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you injured?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got wounded in the leg by two bullets and I was bleeding, but there was nobody to complain to. So when I got to the prison I was still bleeding. I was covered with blood, and my skirt was pierced by those bullets and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. When you heard the shooting, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. When you first heard the shooting as you were tending to your livestock, what action did you take? Did you run? Did you hide? Could you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We did not run. There was shooting. I don't know where from. My man went to the oxen and I went to the sheep. They captured me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before they captured you, were you able to see who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I went to tend to the sheep. I got captured. I don't know who by. I -- they asked me who it was. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you notice anything, anything with respect to the houses in your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, their houses were burning and ours were burning on the 8th. Theirs were burning on Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you said you were captured. Could you tell us who captured you. And when I say "who", could you tell us if they were men, and could you tell us how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were armed men. Though had military gear, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can -- I think this needs to be clarified, Ms. Richardson. She says "on the 7th of January, their houses were burning and ours were burning on the 8th." Perhaps she can explain a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say their houses were burning on the 7th, whose houses and what village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kravica and Mandici were burning on the 7th, and on the 8th, Popovici and Celakovici were burning. That's what burned down on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you know that on the 7th the villages of Kravica and Mandici were burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I know. People started fleeing Kravica and Mandici before the dawn and they started fleeing to Zelinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were able to see this from Popovici, correct, because Popovici is located on a hill? So that we understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Popovici and Mandici are on two hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, as to what the witness could she, she has testified that she couldn't actually see Kravica. If it's a question of seeing people fleeing past her, then perhaps it's a matter that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I thank you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to Kravica, what were you able to see, on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I was being taken through Kravica on the 8th, I could see that Kravica was burnt down completely, and I know that it had burned down on the 7th. And I was taken through Kravica on the 8th, towards Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is clear enough, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think too. Yes, let's proceed, Ms. Richardson, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to your capture, I would like to take you back to that moment that you were captured. You said that there were men who captured you and they were -- were they wearing uniforms? Military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, they wore military uniforms like any other troops. They were armed and there were four of them who captured me, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They slapped me, they shook me, and asked me who, who is it? Who is it? I said I don't know who it is, but I was slapped good and hard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did they ask you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They asked me if I had any cigarettes. I had a pack of cigarettes that I gave them. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where did you get the cigarettes from?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I had it in my house. My house was burning. I went through the flames, to the chest of drawers. I opened the drawer and gave them the cigarettes and then they told me, We didn't kill you, but we're taking you to our commander and he will kill you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you observe who set fire to your house, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The troops that came. They burned my house, but not only mine. They burnt all the houses in the village. Not only mine. The troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you able to see the other houses in the village burning as well as your own?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were all ablaze. They were all burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the four men who captured you, who were dressed in military uniforms, did you see any other men in the area of the houses? And, if you did, could you --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw 400 of them. I heard from them personally that they were 400 of them. They were all armed. They all wore military attire, military clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to where you overheard -- where you heard that there were 400 of them, at the point that you were captured and there were four men at that time dressed in military clothing and there were other houses burning in your village, did you notice any other individuals in the area, in that area where the houses of Popovici are located?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There was nobody else but the troops that came to the village. There was nobody else. Just the troops, the troops that came to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were there any civilians, other -- when I say civilians --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, there were no civilians. Only those in military clothes and armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were these men in military clothing, were they Muslim or Serb? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would ask her whether she knows the -- this is where the distinction between direct and leading questions arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the men dressed in military clothing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know who they were, who they belonged to. They were just troops. Troops -- the troops that came by that set houses -- they set fire to the houses, they just came. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In addition to their uniform, did you notice anything else on them, other than the uniform and the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing else. I did not notice anything else. I could only see military uniforms and weapons that they carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than the green uniform, was there anything else distinctive about the uniforms or anything else that they had that stood out to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They had red bands, some of them around their foreheads and some of them on their shoulders, tied around their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: After you were captured by the four soldiers, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took me to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But before -- and did anything happen once you get -- I will rephrase. They mentioned that they were going to take you to their commander. Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They didn't say who they were taking me to. They said, "We are taking you to the village, to the commander, and it will be up to him whether to kill you or to let you live. We didn't kill you. We will let others do that."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they do that, did they take you to this individual?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The troops gathered in the centre of the village and they then handed me over to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know the name of this commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nezir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this and individual that you knew prior to January 8th?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was a smuggler, Nezir. He traded in cattle. Then he joined the army and he was the commander in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this individual, Nezir, is he Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I told him, "Nezir, please don't let them kill me. And he said "No, I won't let them kill you. You have reached me and I won't let them kill you." And then he gave me the war gear for me to carry to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, how was he dressed? Was he dressed in military or civilian clothing, and can you tell us if he was carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He wore civilian clothes. And he had a hat, a woolen cap, multicoloured hat and civilian clothes, and he wasn't armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did he -- did you observe him doing anything, such as giving orders to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do object to that question, which is very leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes, Mr. Jones. Objection upheld. Ms. Richardson, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You mentioned the four men said that they were taking you to their commander. Did Mr. Nezir introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- as -- let me finish the question. Did Mr. Nezir introduce himself to you as the commander? Or did he give you any title?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They said, "We're taking you to the commander." I asked who the commander is, and it turns out Nezir was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did Nezir say he was the commander to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that. And everybody knew that he was the commander. All the troops that were with him, all the troops knew that he was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said you overheard a conversation or you overheard that there were 400 soldiers. Could you tell us who said this and when?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were talking amongst themselves and they said that there were 400 soldiers in our village. I didn't hear it from anybody else. I heard it from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You also testified that you were given something to carry. Could you explain what that was? And could you also tell us the weight of this - - of whatever it was you were given to carry?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I carried his war gear to Kravica, and I said to Mrs. Golic that I couldn't carry it any more. And then it was taken from me. But to Kravica I carried it myself, and he was the commander responsible for our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to a village that you mentioned, that you testified about previously. You mentioned the village of Celakovici and you said that hamlet was also burning. Could you tell us when it was that you saw this village or hamlet burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Celakovici is the hamlet. It is five or six houses only toward Kravica and it was burnt on the same day as our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was this something you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see it. That's along the road, so I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to see any other villages, whether they're Muslim or Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Our village or -- our villages were burning then. No Muslim villages on the 7th and 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your husband? Was he captured as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. We came from Zelinje and we went to tend to the livestock when the shooting began. So I turned and went to the other direction. He had gone to tend to the oxen, and he found shelter there somewhere, so he wasn't with me at the moment so he was -- and he wasn't caught with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At the time of the attack, was he dressed in military clothing, and did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He didn't have anything. He had no uniform and he wasn't wearing a weapon. He had nothing. And he wasn't a sentry either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to bring you back to where you were captured, and where you had this conversation with Nezir. After this conversation and after he gave you his equipment to carry, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I carried the equipment to Kravica. Then they took it from me. And they took me to Glogova. That's where I spent the night. And then Mrs. Golic took me to Srebrenica, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You mentioned Mrs. Golic, who is that? Who is this person you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: She is from Glogova. She had a brother in the police and so -- and he was on patrol with some of our Serbs and his -- her brother's name was Gojcinovic, and that is what they called her too. She was a nurse, a nurse for that police company.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What ethnicity is she?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: She was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how was it that you came to be with her?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw it in -- I saw, in my village, I saw -- sorry, I saw her and Esma. They were the only women among the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And could you just tell us about their first conversation with Ms. Golic. And is she known by any other name? Does she have another name?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's her maiden name, Fatima Golic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us about your first contact with her.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was good. Like, I had like a friendly conversation with her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did she -- let me just -- I will rephrase that question. When was it that you first saw her, the place?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw her for the first time then. We only met then when she was with the troops there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this was in the middle of the town or was it in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was in the middle of the village. The only women among them were her and Esma. No others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How was Ms. Golic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: She wore jeans, and Esma had white pants and a white ribbon in her hair and she -- she carried a machine-gun, 53-type.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. We just need, Ms. Nikolic, for you to clarify for us. You she'd wore jeans. Who wore jeans? Was this Esma or Ms. Golic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fatima.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So Mrs. Golic wore jeans and a Red Cross bag. And she wore a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And she, meaning who wore a machine-gun? Esma or Ms. Golic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Esma did. And the other only had a Red Cross bag hanging on her, from her shoulder, Ms. Golic that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My next question is with respect to only Ms. Golic. Did she tell you if she was a member of -- who she was with respect to the military?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: She said that she's like military police and that she was carrying this Red Cross bag as a nurse. Fatima did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I let you phrase the question as you did, because there was no objection from the Defence. But please try to avoid putting questions in this fashion. The question should have been: Did she tell you -- did she explain her role there, why she was there, what she was doing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- what she was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She said nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not you. I'm addressing Madam Richardson, not you. I mean you are giving -- you are doing much better than any other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will do my best not to ask leading questions. It is a bit difficult as you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can understand Mr. Jones restraining himself on and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was a matter of restraint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I do appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also have enough feelers to be able to figure out that this can't last much longer and I wouldn't like to have a sitting in which I have Mr. Jones standing up and objecting to every question then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will ask more open-ended questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to Esma, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you knew this individual prior to your meeting with her on January 8th.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I had never heard of her. I didn't know -- didn't know that she was alive, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is she? Or was she?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. She had a machine-gun and she was with the troops, so she would have been a Muslim. What else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did she -- what, if anything, did she say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: See, she only accepted -- accepted me as her brother spent the night in our house sometimes as a police officer, with other police officers, that brother of hers and Brane, the other police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you just testified she only accepted you and her brother spent the night in your house. Are you referring to her brother spent the night in your house. Are you referring to Ms. Golic or Ms. Esma?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, Ms. Golic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to Esma, only Esma, what conversation, if any, did Esma have with you when you met her on January 8th?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't speak to anyone, including her. She was standing apart from most of the others and I was among them. I didn't know who was who and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, did she say anything to you or about you? Esma, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: She only said, "Let me kill her, the fucking Serbian," and Fatima said, "No, you won't kill her. My brother was in her house." And that's what it was between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect, Ms. Richardson. We will have -- I think we can safely have a 30-minute, instead of the usual 25, so that will give her five minutes extra to rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, prior to the break, you testified that you spoke with an Esma and Fatima and that you also were given a bag of -- to carry. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened after this encounter with Fatima and Esma, and where were you taken after this.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Taken? I was taken to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't understand the answer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, you need to repeat your answer, because the interpreters couldn't hear you. If you could speak into the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean where they took me? That was the question? Is that so? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was the following: I will read it out to you. "You have told us about the meeting you had with this Fatima and Esma and that you were also given a bag of -- a bag to carry." Madam Richardson asked you whether you could tell us now, what happened after this, after this encounter with Fatima and Esma, and where were you taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean where we were taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Esma and Fatima Golic, I don't remember -- I don't know the last name of Esma. But Fatima Golic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Where did they take you? Or where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They took me through Kravica, so I was taken through Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there, Ms. Nikolic. As you were being taken through Kravica, were you walking?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you the only prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The only one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many -- who was with you, other than Fatima and Esma?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell how many troops there were?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. In the village there were -- there were many troops. More than in our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: As you were walking through Kravica, what were you able to observe with respect to the condition of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we were passing through Kravica, we found five dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you recognise -- what was the condition of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were four soldiers and one woman and one was without a head.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of the bodies? Was it anyone that you knew?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew a man from Krajici, Gordan Nikolic, the son of Cvijetin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is he? Was he? Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mean Gordan, the son of Cvijetin?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that he was -- he was a soldier when he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, was he Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the condition of the town of Kravica itself or the areas that you observed, the houses, could you tell us what condition they were?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. As I was passing through, or before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: As you were passing through.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All the houses were burnt and nothing was -- had been left standing. It had all been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after leaving Kravica, where did you go next? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To Krajici, where there were the five dead bodies, and up to Glogova and that's where they took me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in Glogova, how long did you stay? And who were you with?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I spent the night there and they took me to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say "they", who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the troops, those who were taking me. I don't know which troops they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the house of the Nikolic family in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were the Nikolics present?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, they had left. They had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the following day, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But he took me away anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, after leaving Glogova, where were you taken, do you remember, the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took me away. I don't know which road it was. On the 10th, when we went to Potocari. Or, no, no, it wasn't the 10th. It was on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you went to Potocari -- you were taken to Potocari the day after spending the night in Glogova, the next day?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. In the morning Fatima took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And where is the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What time did you get to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We arrived there at 8.00, from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was that in the morning or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Had you been to Potocari -- excuse me. Had you been to Srebrenica prior to this day?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother had a house there and I had -- and I had stayed with him sometimes, but not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you arrived in the police station, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened. I found --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name from Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- who was captured there and I was there with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of this person that you met over there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean -- it was Dostana Obramovic, from Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where were you held in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They took me to a room and kept me there. And once there were more women, they took us to the prison in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before we get to the prison and the other women, who was in the room when you first arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The police were there. It was a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember how many of them were there? How many police were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were. They took me to a room, but I don't remember how many they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to taking you to the room, did they ask you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. What would they have asked me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who else was in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I found her, and another 12 women were also brought to the police station from other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "her", are you referring to Dostana?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How soon after did the other women arrive? Was it a day later or more than a day?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was on Orthodox New Year when 12 more women were brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of these women that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any children present?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Children? Yes, I think there were five children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember if they were boys or girls?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: One -- one girl, and there was one boy by the name of Branko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you said you don't remember the names of the women who were brought in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement in the year 2000 to an investigator? And there was an interpreter present.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Just think back for a moment. In 2000, did someone come to speak to you about what had happened to you in Srebrenica, and what had happened in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, other than -- prior to coming here, if you think back about four years ago, did someone come to you or were you taken somewhere, where you were asked about what had happened in 1993 in your village and what had happened when you were in the police station in Srebrenica. Do you remember? Not what you said to them, but do you remember what they came and they spoke to you about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to -- is this the first time that you have spoken about what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, after you were released from prison in 1993, did anyone speak to you then?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they did or whether they didn't. I'd sooner say that they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, we would prefer that you tell us. If you don't remember, you can say that -- you should say that you don't remember, and if you don't know, you can let us know that you don't know as well. So my question is, if you listen carefully, do you recall, in 2000 - you may not remember the year, but a few years prior to today - that someone came and spoke to you. That person was possibly speaking English Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and there was someone else who spoke your language, who translated what he -- what he was saying and what he asked you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it wasn't a "he".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. And I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember an interpreter by the name of Zeljka?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik, you mean? There was an interpreter called Zeljka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened in Zvornik? Let's -- what happened in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A policeman came from Bratunac and he took me to Zvornik, and there I gave a statement. And she was there to interview me. She was like somebody foreign, and there was an interpreter with her. That was in Zvornik. That's where I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to whom did you give this statement? Do you know who had sent them there? Do you know who had sent them there to speak to you, to interview you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who sent them. They just asked me to go to Zvornik. Our police took them there, brought me back home. I went there. I told them what I knew. And there was this foreign woman with -- Zeljka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you told them what had happened to you in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also told them about the women who had been in prison with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAVA NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were women. And I don't know -- I did tell them about them, and I told you about them, about these women that were with me. I told you yesterday about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, since the witness does not read or write, I would like to read from the 2000 statement, the list of names and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I think we're very far from having established a foundation for that. Apart from the fact that the witness on many occasions said she doesn't know, doesn't remember, we're far from identifying, as the 2000 statement, this Zvornik statement. And as Your Honour is probably aware, there is a statement which is identified as being from Zvornik, which is from 1994. The 2000 statement doesn't say anywhere that it was taken in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It never does, actually, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. And so, in my submission, this witness hasn't given evidence that she recalls making the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't say any more, Mr. Jones, especially since the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think for the time being, there are these problems, Ms. Richardson. I think it is too early for you to refer to the statement before you clear a few other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because -- and I can explain to you. I mean, there is a diagram, the origin of which is explained in the statement. There is a statement at the end of the statement which says that the witness signed her signature, where indicated. Instead -- there is a mark, and there is nothing accompanying that mark which attests to whom it belongs. I mean, there are a few things that you need to cover first before I can tell you, Yes, Ms. Richardson, now you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm fully aware there are a number of steps for the refreshing exercise to be completed. It's very apparent it is quite painful at this point. But if the Court -- if you would have me go through them, we can maybe -- we may be here for a while going through it but we can attempt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can try to help you a little bit, but only a little bit, in order to see whether we could proceed. Madam Nikolic, look at me, please. Yes. You told us that when you got to the police station, you met a woman there, another Serb, by the name of Dostana. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You also told us that later on another number of women arrived, something like 12 women arrived; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also told us that there were a number of children, and you remembered particularly a small boy, a young boy by the name of Branko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there was a little girl. Do you remember her name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Her mother's name was Stana and her name was Vesna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So now, again now we have two women there that you have given us the name of, Dostana and Stana. Do you remember the names of the other women that were there? You can take them one by one at your leisure and pleasure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were just those that I mentioned to the Prosecutor yesterday. There were 12, the three of us were there, the daughter in law and there were three children who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But now Mrs. Nikolic, you need to help me a little bit, because, as you can confirm, I was not with you yesterday when you were telling these names to Ms. Richardson. So if I wasn't there, I need you to help me a little bit now and give me the same names that you gave to Ms. Richardson. Can we go through the list one by one, you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can, if that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is very much necessary. So you told us Dostana and you told us Stana. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
